articles.title: Manic Street Preachers frontman feels 'more pressure' playing in Wales
articles.summary: The Welsh rock band will headline Blackweir Fields in Cardiff on Saturday 19 June 2027.
articles.body:
Manic Street Preachers frontman James Dean Bradfield said playing in Wales brings "extra pressure" as the band prepare to mark 35 years of their debut album.

The band will headline Blackweir Fields in Cardiff next summer, performing the landmark 1992 record Generation Terrorists in full.

Bradfield said their rock songs about banking, environmental damage and ideology still "have a prescience for anything you could talk about now".

He said when the band wrote the album, which sold 250,000 copies worldwide upon its release, they were "a bit unreasonable and a bit mad" but also "fiercely ambitious".

Bradfield, raised in Blackwood, Caerphilly, said the album was shaped by the decline of the south Wales valleys after pit closures, channeling their surroundings into songs such as Nat West-Barclays-Midlands-Lloyds, Slash N Burn and Crucifix Kiss.

While discussing Nat West-Barclays-Midlands-Lloyds, he said: "That song has a prescient nature about it and it always will."

"Even though it dates itself, you can take some of the songs and you can actually trace them over the times that we live in now."

Bradfield joked that he and his band mates Nicky Wire, Sean Moore and the late Richey Edwards were "fun to hang out with, I promise you".

The album also features Little Baby Nothing, which Bradfield originally envisioned Kylie Minogue singing.

"She did sing on stage with us once in the Shepherd's Bush Empire. I think that was during the Everything Must Go tour, and she was brilliant," he said.

Previously, Bradfield translated one of their songs from their fifth album, This Is My Truth Tell Me Yours, into Welsh for a S4C music series.

"It was a challenge to sing Ready for Drowning in Welsh, definitely," he said.

"I tried to do the lyric justice in Welsh as much as it had been done justice in English.

"I tried to keep it as poetic as possible rather than just the facts."

Bradfield said playing at home in Wales was "a privilege" but came with "more pressure" than gigs elsewhere.

"You can't hide away from the fact that there's more pressure and there's a lot more tension around a hometown gig.

"All those pressures add into making it, it feels like there's more at stake."

"You might see people on the dog walk that came to the concert the night before," he said, laughing.

"You don't want them to give you a bad review when you're getting a coffee with your dog."

He also admitted that he sometimes worries about the prospect of family members being in the crowd and swearing on stage.

"One of my uncles or aunties are going to be in the crowd and I better watch my language. And you're thinking, what am I talking about? I'm in a band," he said.

Asked which songs younger fans should start with, Bradfield picked Crucifix Kiss, Nat West-Barclays-Midlands-Lloyds and So Dead, a song they have never played live.

"Those three songs in themselves, I think, still have a prescience for anything you could talk about now."

Discussing their one-night performance next June, Bradfield said he felt "nervous" about playing the full album and had already started rehearsing.

"I think they can expect a band that's very, very tight, pretty aggressive, but we're going to be on message in terms of the record that we're representing."

He added: "It's going to be very faithful."

Bradfield told fans to expect Wire "to really be rocking the leopard print more than you could imagine."

The Libertines, The Cardigans and The Tub will also be supporting the band on Saturday 19 June 2027.

He added: "We've got to try and find a way to honour Richey as well."

Edwards, from Blackwood, disappeared on 1 February 1995.

His car was found abandoned near the old Severn Bridge , but no trace of him has ever been found, and he was declared legally dead in 2008.

articles.title: Andy Taylor obituary: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off
articles.summary: How a wayward child from the north-east of England made it with the world's biggest band.
articles.body:
Andy Taylor, who has died aged 65, was the wild boy of Duran Duran.

In the early 1980s, the pop legends sold over 100 million records and dominated the charts in both Britain and the United States.

But success came at a cost. For Taylor, global superstardom became a cocaine and alcohol fuelled nightmare that left him burnt out and battling clinical depression.

"For sure, we paraded around in our fast cars with beautiful models on yachts in the south of France without needing to pay the bill," he later wrote.

Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies, aged 65

Andrew Taylor was born in North Tyneside on 16 February 1961.

Home was Cullercoats, a coastal village near Whitley Bay where many people, including his uncles, depended on the sea for their livelihoods.

"It was like Coronation Street," he said, "with fish."

At first, it was a happy childhood. There was church on Sunday with his parents, Ronnie and Blanche, followed by games of football on the beach with younger brother Ronnie junior.

On Christmas Day, his extended family would belt out Bing Crosby hits around the piano.

Everything changed on his first day at grammar school.

The 11-year-old returned home to find his father in the kitchen, silently weeping. Taylor's mother, it seemed, had simply disappeared. There wasn't even a note.

"It was like a guillotine had suddenly come rushing down," he recalled. It "sliced everything apart without explanation as to why I was guilty".

After that, occasional meetings with his mother were chilly encounters with no explanation offered. Taylor never discovered why she had left.

Having worked hard to pass his 11-plus exams, Taylor rapidly went off the rails.

He skipped school and spent many days in remote caves on the beach, drinking cider and smoking dried banana skins. He'd heard absurd rumours this would get him high.

Salvation lay in a guitar he found hidden in his father's cupboard and a BBC Two programme that taught him the basic chords.

By the age of 16, he was working on a building site and playing in a band.

Taylor and his friends performed at working men's clubs across the north-east of England, often providing musical accompaniment for strippers.

A contract to provide entertainment for American troops in Germany included a clause stipulating that he did six hours a night on stage.

In return, the soldiers introduced him to marijuana.

On his return, Taylor saw an advert seeking a "livewire guitarist" for a new band based in the West Midlands.

He called the number and "made that fateful train journey to Birmingham".

Duran Duran, named after a character in Jane Fonda's space-sex movie Barbarella, were to be based in a club called the Rum Runner.

On arrival, he met bassist John Taylor and drummer Roger Taylor - all unrelated.

Keyboardist Nick Rhodes followed and, after a short search, Simon Le Bon, the lead singer, appeared "looking like an Elvis who'd been to the chip shop".

They didn't waste time. Within six weeks, the group had pulled together enough material for an album.

Andy Taylor's musical challenge was to work out how his guitar fitted a post-punk age of electronic music, while Le Bon's lyrics and melody skated over the top.

A record deal with EMI gave the group the production support they needed.

Planet Earth was released on 21 February 1981. It raced towards the top 10, winning them a coveted slot on Top of the Pops.

Six months later, Girls on Film reached number five in the UK charts.

The New Romantic revolution, as much about fashion as music, was under way.

The boys discovered that their Antony Price suits and make-up gave them something to talk about with girls in the clubs.

And there were soon girls everywhere, thanks to a marketing campaign that pushed the band heavily in teen magazines.

After one US concert, the band swept the stage and supposedly counted 2,000 teddy bears, 150 pairs of knickers, 300 bras and dozens of hotel room keys that had been thrown from the crowd.

The music itself was cheerful, catchy and aspirational.

"We were just working-class escapists who wanted to live out our dreams," explained Taylor. "We didn't want to be like UB40 and The Specials singing about unemployment and urban decay."

Duran Duran embarked on exhausting foreign tours to drive sales, and their flamboyant videos, made at huge cost, played constantly on MTV in the US.

A bandmate pushed Taylor off a yacht while shooting the video for Rio, and he nearly drowned off the Caribbean coast amid a swarm of poisonous jellyfish.

In Sri Lanka, the group was forced to flee when 4,000 furious monks objected to their using a holy site as a backdrop to Hungry Like the Wolf.

Then, having smoked dope and drunk a bottle of Jack Daniel's, Taylor climbed a tree with his guitar for a spectacular shot.

He fell into a muddy lagoon that was used by local elephants as a latrine and spent four days in hospital recovering from a tropical infection.

By now, Taylor's original £50-a-week retainer from EMI was a distant memory.

He shared a flat in Moseley with Le Bon, took prodigious quantities of cocaine, and worked his way through the flocks of page three girls who frequented the Rum Runner.

Then he met Tracey Wilson, a level-headed hair salon manager.

Initially, she had doubts about becoming romantically involved with a self-confessed womanising, drug-taking guitarist.

She was eventually persuaded and, on his 21st birthday, Taylor proposed. The couple remained together for more than 40 years and had four children.

Famously, Duran Duran were Princess Diana's favourite band. This too, came with risks.

In June 1983, the IRA tried to assassinate the Prince and Princess of Wales while they watched the group perform live at Tottenham Court Road's Dominion Theatre.

The plot, which involved planting a bomb in the toilets, was stopped by British intelligence.

Fortunately, the IRA man sent to plant the device turned out to be a double agent, who tipped off MI5 and fled to Paris.

The same year, Is There Something I Should Know? became Duran Duran's fastest-selling song to date.

The Reflex, which their record company initially refused to release, also topped the charts on both sides of the Atlantic.

The American press called them the Fab Five, in comparison to the Beatles, and their vast earnings caused them to become tax exiles.

For Andy Taylor, foreign tours had become increasingly drug-fuelled with so-called "rock docs" injecting him with chemicals to get through sets.

The constant use of cocaine made him nervy and irrational. The BBC threatened to ban him from their Saturday Superstore programme when he swore at a caller.

Headlines about Taylor's drug use at the Rum Runner damaged the band's hitherto squeaky-clean image.

In Birmingham, the club was suddenly served with a compulsory purchase order by the council and bulldozed.

Their Wild Boys video featured Simon Le Bon strapped to a huge waterwheel. But it was Andy Taylor who felt as if he was drowning.

As a guitarist, he wanted to make records with a harder rock edge, which led to The Power Station - a band he put together with Robert Palmer while killing time between Duran Duran tours.

But it was his lifestyle that was worrying him. After years of living on Big Macs and cocaine, he knew he was heading for a breakdown.

After Live Aid in 1985, the constant bickering between members of the band led to a prolonged separation.

When they ran out of money, Duran Duran's original line-up reformed to work on new projects.

They continued to sell plenty of tickets for live shows to die-hard fans, but new records had disappointing sales.

By the time the group made Red Carpet Massacre, their 12th album, Taylor had decided to quit.

In 2006, Duran Duran released a statement saying there was "an unworkable gulf between us and we can no longer effectively function together".

The best Andy Taylor could say about Red Carpet Massacre was that it "sounded as if it had been recorded in a hurry".

Having weaned himself off drugs, he moved to Ibiza and set up a scheme to help unsigned artists release music while retaining their profits.

In 2022, it was announced that he had advanced prostate cancer, the same disease that had killed his father.

Le Bon spoke for the remaining members of the group. "It's absolutely devastating," he said.

Taylor avoided chemotherapy, believing it would affect his guitar playing by weakening his fingers. Instead, he embarked on an experimental "nuclear therapy", which he hoped would give him five more years of life.

Initially, at least, it seemed successful but, a year later, Le Bon said his former bandmate's disease was a "very late, fourth-stage metastasised cancer".

In 2025, Taylor managed to release a third solo album, Man's a Wolf to A Man. Urged by Tracey to express himself for a final time, he even provided the vocals.

For Andy Taylor, that first train ride down to Birmingham had been like entering Narnia in the Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe.

Overnight, he had gone from serenading strippers in northern clubs to a rock-star lifestyle with the world's most popular band.

So, was the rollercoaster ride worth it? Taylor answered his own question in his autobiography, published in 2008.

"Maybe if there'd been fewer lows there wouldn't have been so many highs," he wrote. "If I had to do it all over again, I don't think I would have changed a thing.

"Though next time I'll give a miss to swallowing all that elephant's piss," he added.

articles.title: Trump slaps new tariffs on 14 nations; India faces additional 17%
articles.summary: Setting the stage for additional duty burden on exports, the US Trade Representative on Wednesday proposed 17 per cent additional tariffs on Indian goods,
articles.body: Setting the stage for additional duty burden on exports, the US Trade Representative on Wednesday proposed 17 per cent additional tariffs on Indian goods, which can rise to 25 per cent if the bilateral trade deal is not signed.Citing the findings of its Section 301 investigation against 16 countries for alleged structural excess capacity, the Trump administration has proposed additional levies of 15-20 per cent against 14 offending countries, with the developed nations at the lower end of the band and China, Vietnam and Singapore at the top. The move, though not surprising, creates fresh complications for exporters, with two important exports from India, pharma and mobile phones, exempted from additional tariffs.While most developing countries are in the 18 per cent bracket, India has a one-percentage-point “comparative advantage”, provided the first tranche of the agreement which was finalised last Feb, is signed by the time the final hearings are completed and tariffs are announced. With the hearings scheduled on Jan 25, 2027, the fresh levies are likely to kick in next Feb. In India’s case, the probe flagged PLI schemes as part of the Atmanirbhar Bharat push and sector-specific acts, policies and practices in the steel, solar, health and ICT sectors.Government rejects structural excess capacity chargeThe government on Wednesday rejected charges of structural excess capacity in any sector, and said it will work with the US for early conclusion of a bilateral trade agreement. “India and the US are engaged in negotiations for a BTA. articles.title: The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade is postponed due to a storm. It’s not the first time weather has made its mark.
articles.summary: Today's wind restrictions stem directly from past problems.
articles.body:
With stormy weather bearing down on New York, the annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed on Wednesday for the first time in its 100-year history . It will now take place on Saturday instead.

But while the event itself had never technically been delayed — until now — bad weather has bedeviled organizers and attendees before. Some of this is just the law of averages. Late November is a relatively rainy period in the Big Apple, with measurable precipitation falling 25% to 30% of the time. It's also peak season for major coastal storms.

This week's storm — an extratropical cyclone along the East Coast — is expected to bring "strong to damaging wind gusts" and "widespread moderate to locally heavy rainfall," according to the National Weather Service . Wind maps show that those gusts could hit 40 mph in the morning and peak at more than 50 mph during the afternoon .

That's why this year's parade has been pushed back: The city's safety rules stipulate that large balloons — the event's signature attraction — must be grounded if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts surpass 34 mph.

And those wind restrictions stem directly from past problems.

In 1993, strong gusts sent a Sonic the Hedgehog balloon careening into a lamppost at Columbus Circle; a piece of the lamp pulled off by the punctured balloon injured a child and an off-duty police officer .

Then, in 1997, organizers and city officials learned how bad things can get when giant inflatables encounter 43 mph wind gusts in the valley-like gaps between Manhattan's high-rises.

That year, a six-story Cat in the Hat balloon collided with a lamppost at 72nd Street and Central Park West and sent debris raining to the ground. Metal pieces wound up striking a paradegoer, fracturing her skull and leaving her in a coma for 24 days. Three others were injured as well. Then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani formed a task force in response, and that task force came up with today's wind rules, among other safety measures. (They also temporarily removed lamppost arms along the parade route.)

The woman whose skull was fractured later filed a lawsuit seeking nearly $400 million in damages. The case was settled in 2001 for an undisclosed amount.

In 2005, an M&M balloon ripped open when it struck a light pole. Pieces of the pole broke off, causing minor injuries to two spectators.

In 2006, paradegoers endured nearly 2 inches of rain; in 2019, wind gusts hit 33 mph, right near the limit. In both cases, balloons were flown closer to the ground. Organizers installed wind measurement devices along the parade route to monitor changing conditions, and the taller, upright balloons were rotated into a horizontal, downward position for safety.

The snowiest parade on record occurred in 1989, when more than 4 inches of frozen fluff fell by noon. The coldest came in 2018, with frigid temperatures of 17 degrees Fahrenheit (exacerbated by winds up to 20 mph).

But each time, the show went on as scheduled.

In fact, before this year, only two things had ever really disrupted the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. One was war: The event was not held from 1942 to 1944, while the U.S. was fighting in World War II.

The other was (you guessed it) weather. In 1971, a serious storm pummeled New York City. A little more than an inch of rain fell, along with a dusting of snow. But the wind gusts hit a whopping 63 mph in Central Park . All of the parade's giant balloons were grounded as a result.

articles.title: Lamp not lit atop deepathoon, Supreme Court to hear contempt case
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu government’s failure to comply with the Supreme Court’s order to allow the lighting of the traditional Karthigai Deepam lamp atop
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu government’s failure to comply with the Supreme Court’s order to allow the lighting of the traditional Karthigai Deepam lamp atop deepathoon as a one-time arrangement may lead to contempt proceedings.On Wednesday, the Supreme Court said it would hear the contempt case despite the Madurai Collector’s apology to the court. A fresh petition has also been filed seeking directions to light the lamp atop deepathoon, the disputed stone pillar atop Thiruparankundram hill in Madurai.Appearing for the Collector, senior advocate Gopal Sankarnarayanan told a bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul Pancholi that the court’s order could not be carried out and the lamp was not lit at the assigned place. He also said the Collector had filed a report.The non-compliance stood out against the backdrop of opposition to the lighting of the lamp atop the deepathoon from Sikandar Badusha Dargah Committee, state government, its Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department, the Madurai district administration, and the Temple Board of Trustees.An array of political parties TVK as well as its predecessor in office, DMK, Congress, Left parties and Muslim outfits, have been opposing the move.Collector apologises for lamp not being lit atop DeepathoonIn a twist to the controversy, the temple administration’s explanation for retaining the customary lighting venue came under question after four sthanikars (traditional temple priests) said their communication regarding lighting the lamp near Uchi Pillaiyar temple was sent last year and that they had submitted no letter regarding this year’s festival. The trustees had cited the priests’ views as one of the reasons for their decision to light the lamp at the customary spot.Senior advocate Guru Krishna Kumar, appearing for the petitioner, told the SC bench there was a “deliberate attempt” not to comply with the apex court’s directive. Kumar again told the bench in the afternoon that a devotee had filed a fresh plea seeking a directive to light the deepam atop the disputed Deepathoon with the flame from the lamp lit Tuesday. The court said it would hear this plea too.Meanwhile, a litigant made a mention before Madras HC seeking to initiate suo motu contempt proceedings over non-compliance with SC’s directive.In the status report, the Madurai collector said he had made all efforts to comply with SC’s directive, and he should not be blamed for failure to do so. “I submit that I took all the steps to comply with the order in good faith....I sincerely apologise for the lamp not being lit at the Deepathoon. The district administration made every effort to secure the authorisation of the Devasthanam and the lighting of the lamp at the Deepathoon. However, the board of trustees resolved to light the lamp at the customary place,” the report said.SC had allowed the lighting of the traditional lamp at Deepathoon on Nov 24 as a one-time measure and directed only authorised persons to attend the ceremony.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Fighting against BJP or us?’ Congress slams Samajwadi Party over its list
articles.summary: LUCKNOW/DELHI/MEERUT: Congress MP Imran Masood questioned Wednesday whether Samajwadi Party intended to fight BJP or Congress after SP announced five
articles.body: LUCKNOW/DELHI/MEERUT: Congress MP Imran Masood questioned Wednesday whether Samajwadi Party intended to fight BJP or Congress after SP announced five candidates, including four sitting MLAs, while seat-sharing talks for the 2027 UP polls were still under way, triggering a fresh flashpoint between the allies.SP had offered Congress 26 constituencies against its wish-list of 131 as seat-sharing negotiations stretched to 3.5 hours in New Delhi on Tuesday, considerably longer than Monday’s 15-minute opening round. Later at night, SP announced its list of five, putting the alliance under strain.Masood said Congress was SP’s ally, “not a beggar”, and warned that if it could announce candidates during negotiations, his party could do the same. “When you make such an announcement against me, I don’t understand whether you want to fight me, Congress, or BJP,” he said.Want Akhilesh as CM, but won’t settle for less than 100 seats: CongressMasood took exception to SP’s list, which included candidates from Behat and Saharanpur. Congress is said to have sought both these seats, with Masood representing Saharanpur in Lok Sabha.SP sought to contain the fallout, dismissing Masood’s remarks as personal and insisting the candidate announcement was not unilateral. Ghosi MP Rajiv Rai said the two parties had agreed that constituencies held by sitting MLAs would not be part of seat-sharing negotiations, while Sambhal MP Zia-ur-Rehman Barq said SP had received no such objection from Congress as a party.“As far as the issue of Imran Masood Sahib’s displeasure is concerned, I believe that, for the time being, it is a personal matter. We have not received any such message from our party or Congress,” the Sambhal MP said.SP chief Akhilesh Yadav had sought to ease tensions Tuesday, describing the 2027 polls as a “historic opportunity” for the allies to jointly take on BJP. He said seat-sharing should hinge on winnability rather than quotas and indicated the 26 seats offered to Congress so far were not the final tally.AICC in-charge for UP Rajendra Pal Gautam backed Masood’s objection, calling the announcement premature. “This was wrong. It should not have been done. As a responsible political party, they should have waited. The list could have been announced after the discussions concluded. There was no urgency.”Gautam said Congress’s MP for Saharanpur made it imperative for the constituency to be discussed before candidates were named. He nevertheless described the 3.5-hour negotiations as positive and reiterated Congress’s demand for a “respectable” share, saying the party would not settle for fewer than 100 of UP’s 403 seats. Congress wanted Akhilesh to become CM, but would not compromise on its workers’ dignity or organisational interests, he said.Congress Legislature Party functionary Virendra Chaudhary called SP’s announcement a “violation of gathbandhan dharma”, while UP Congress president Aradhana Misra declined to comment.The allies had won a combined 43 Lok Sabha seats in UP in 2024, with SP securing 37 and Congress six. But the assembly seat-sharing bargain has proved more difficult as Congress seeks to rebuild its organisation and SP protects its sitting MLAs and electoral strongholds.SP is set to unveil the first of its election manifestos Thursday, with youth, education, social justice, Dalit issues, agriculture, farmers, law and order, industry and MSMEs among the key themes. A separate manifesto focused on women is expected later.SP’s early candidate announcement also brought Kairana back into focus with the renomination of three-time MLA Nahid Hasan, who won the seat in 2022 while in jail following his arrest under the Gangsters Act. He defeated his nearest rival by nearly 25,000 votes and secured bail from Allahabad HC in Dec 2022. His sister Iqra Hasan won Kairana’s Lok Sabha seat in 2024, defeating BJP’s Pradeep Chaudhary by more than 69,000 votes.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Florida jury awarded $6 million to the wife and two daughters of Carlos Chalbaud, who died on the operating table during elective neck surgery at Holy Cross Hospital without clearance from a cardiologist
articles.summary: A routine medical procedure intended to address a neck condition ended in tragedy for a Florida family, turning an elective surgery into a fatal medical
articles.body: A routine medical procedure intended to address a neck condition ended in tragedy for a Florida family, turning an elective surgery into a fatal medical negligence case. More than three years after 52-year-old Carlos Chalbaud suffered cardiac arrest on the operating table, a Broward County jury has held the hospital and medical professionals responsible, awarding $6 million to his wife and two daughters over failures surrounding his preoperative assessment and surgical care.The verdict followed a three-week trial, with jurors' deliberations interrupted by a two-day courthouse closure caused by severe flooding. According to the Miami Herald, the decision was delivered on Friday, following the proceedings in Broward County.Abnormal heart test, surgery anywayAccording to Morning Star report, Chalbaud had elective cervical stenosis surgery at Holy Cross Hospital in Fort Lauderdale on April 3, 2023. However, his preoperative electrocardiogram (EKG) showed abnormalities, and a cardiologist declined to provide surgical clearance, recommending a comprehensive cardiac evaluation instead.CBS 12 reported that the lawsuit claimed the recommended assessment was never done.However, nurse practitioner Glenda W Thomas cleared Chalbaud for general anesthesia, saying he had no medical contraindications. The surgery subsequently proceeded despite the absence of the requested cardiology clearance.Overseeing Chalbaud during surgery was another issue during the trial. His blood pressure and heart rate reportedly declined for approximately 30 minutes before his heart stopped, the online report added.Morning Star reported that the anaesthesia record contained a gap of around 17 minutes during which no vital signs were documented, becoming a significant element of the family's negligence case.Hospital and medical team held responsibleThe lawsuit named Holy Cross Hospital, Thomas and members of the anaesthesia team, including physician Robert A. Drozd and certified registered nurse anaesthetist Larisa Turetsky.Following the trial, jurors assigned 30% liability to the nurse practitioner, 60% to the anaesthesiology team and the remaining 10% to the hospital.According to the Sun Sentinel, the jury determined that the failures by the medical providers contributed to Chalbaud's death, resulting in a combined $6 million award for his immediate family. The proceedings were overseen by Senior Judge Carlos Rodriguez. Jurors began deliberations on November 17, but severe flooding forced the courthouse to close for two days before they returned to deliver their decision.Wife and daughters receive $6 million awardChalbaud's wife, Anabella Acosta, and their daughters, Miranda and Sofia, were each awarded $2 million in damages. The jury also granted an additional $20,000 to cover medical and funeral expenses, according to Morning Star.The family's history was also presented during the proceedings. Chalbaud and Acosta married in Venezuela in 2003 before relocating to Maryland in 2018 to provide better educational opportunities for their daughters. He had built a career in the corporate sector, eventually becoming chief operating officer at Vepica, and obtained US citizenship three months before his death.The verdict brings a significant legal development for the family, whose case centred on whether medical providers should have proceeded with an elective operation despite abnormal cardiac findings and the absence of specialist clearance.Image Courtesy: Google GeminiYou use AI every day. articles.title: Pier collapses, seawalls breached, homes flooded as big waves, historic high tides hit California
articles.summary: The damage was greatest in the coastal town of Pacifica, where relentless waves sent water streaming down several city blocks and collapsed a section of the...
articles.body:
Pier collapses, seawalls breached, homes flooded as big waves, historic high tides hit California

Coastal California communities were deluged Wednesday by powerful waves and record-breaking high tides, breaching seawalls, flooding some homes and causing a chunk of a pier south of San Francisco to collapse amid 20- to 30-foot waves.

The damage was greatest in the coastal town of Pacifica, where relentless waves sent water streaming down several city blocks and collapsed a section of the historic pier. A massive swell of ocean water struck the perpendicular portion of the L-shaped pier, causing the vertical supports to suddenly buckle.

King tides — fueled by a historic El Niño , record hot ocean temperatures and strong swells coming from the west — set all-time high tide levels in parts of Southern California, flooding multiple homes in Orange County.

"This El Niño is unprecedented with its strength," said San Mateo County Supervisor Ray Mueller. "For this to be happening when it is a beautiful day on the coastside today, in clear sunshine and no wind, is really significant."

As salt water poured over carefully-lined rows of sandbags and inundated multiple homes in Pacifica — where floodwaters were knee-high on some streets by midday — Mueller told The Times that pumps that were supposed to remove floodwaters were all operational, but overwhelmed by the amount of water coming over the seawall.

"They're having a hard time keeping up with the water that's coming over," Mueller said, noting that local officials will need help with the recovery. "We really are going to need resources to shore up this entire area. And frankly, these pumps are going to need to be fixed as well, so that they're operating better."

The section of the Pacifica pier that collapsed Wednesday had come down in previous storms, Mueller said, so it was "not completely unexpected that that section would come down." Built in 1973, the pier had most recently been closed in June after crews observed cracks running through the landmark structure.

Gov. Gavin Newsom said the damage in Pacifica was "heartbreaking."

"This is a preview of things to come," Newsom told reporters in San Francisco. "This is anomalous today. This is normal tomorrow. This is what our kids will experience every day, and that's why it's so important that we not just situationally address moments like this, but sustainably get under the hood and try to solve some of these things."

While temporary flood barriers are helping coastal areas up and down the state, Newsom said, they would not ultimately be enough. "That's not the solution to these longer-term trend lines," he warned.

On California's Central Coast, the Santa Cruz County Sheriff's Office issued a shelter-in-place order Wednesday for Pajaro Dunes resort, a small beachside community, "due to high water levels." In Stinson Beach in Marin County, evacuation warnings were issued for beachfront homes, while shelter-in-place orders went into effect for neighboring roads.

As 24-foot waves slammed into the Point Reyes area, the National Weather Service Bay Area urged residents to exercise caution: "Life-threatening surf, strong rip currents and localized coastal erosion expected," the agency posted on X. "Remain away from the shoreline — do NOT venture onto jetties, piers or rocks!"

Big waves slammed into beachfront buildings on Capitola village, south of Santa Cruz, flooding some streets.

And in Monterey County, officials closed multiple beaches, warning in a news release that waves could reach as high as 50 feet.

Communities across California have been frantically preparing for coastal flooding for weeks after officials warned that major flooding could inundate the coast on Thanksgiving week, peaking Wednesday and Thursday.

As residents worked to fortify homes and businesses with tarps and sandbags, some cities and counties closed beaches, issued evacuation warnings and dispatched crews to inspect stormwater infrastructure, install flood barriers and reinforce seawalls.

With California facing more exceptional king tides after Thanksgiving week is over — around Christmas and then Martin Luther King Jr. Day — Mueller said residents should prepare for the possibility of even more intense damage.

"Imagine everything we have today, but with a storm system on top of it," he said. "As soon as we get this cleared out, that is what we start to prepare for, because this was a practice drill for what could come."

In Southern California, high tides brought problems to some communities.

In San Diego, preliminary data showed the coastal neighborhood of La Jolla recorded a high tide of 8.11 feet, exceeding the previous record of 7.98 feet set on Oct. 27. Santa Barbara recorded a high tide of 8.21 feet, breaking the old record of 8.04 feet. In Los Angeles, the harbor tide gauge in San Pedro hit 8.19 feet, tying the record set last month. Monterey posted a record sea height of 8.02 feet, breaking the record of 7.95 feet set on Jan. 27, 1983.

Despite the immense damage in parts of Northern California, the sea level did not break records in San Francisco, peaking Wednesday at 8.21 feet, just shy of Tuesday's observation of 8.23 feet.

In Orange County, Eric McCoy, Huntington Beach's fire chief, said that multiple homes flooded in Sunset Beach and crews were assessing damage after high tides of 8.3 feet deluged the coastline. In some areas, he said, water had breached seawalls and docks and boats breached pilings.

Still, McCoy told reporters, even though the tides were higher Wednesday than they were in October, the city experienced less damage.

Residents had mitigated the flooding, he said, by taking significant measures to protect their homes. The public works department had also taken several steps it had never taken before, such as putting ladders in drains and sandbagging seawalls.

Tony Nobles, president of the Sunset Beach Community Assn., agreed that residents had taken "extraordinary measures" to protect their homes. He and other volunteers helped set up sandbag walls for people who couldn't do it themselves, he said, helping secure 35 homes and five businesses.

"They learned a lot in October," Nobles said. "The houses that were well protected didn't get wet."

On Wednesday morning, Nobles was picking up a water pump he'd delivered to help a resident pump out water when he got a call on his cellphone from an elderly couple whose home he'd helped protect. The couple has three properties that got water damage in October.

"You guys stayed dry, right?" Nobles said, leaning against the tailgate of his pickup truck. "Wonderful."

On Bayview Drive, Gary Scott, 71, was plainly pleased with all the work he had done in recent weeks to fortify his home — especially since his efforts last month did not stop water from seeping into his ground floor and causing extensive damage.

Scott spent $10,000 on a retaining wall between his house and a neighbor's property, and spent days with his son and his son's friends filling and hauling about 240 sandbags to block off the front side of his property with a wall that was five bags tall.

Like the city, Scott had learned from the last major flooding. The bags he'd installed in October weren't high enough that time, so the water poured through them and flooded the first floor of his home. Water also came in from his next-door neighbor's property, he said. Even though the first floor remained dry, a musty smell still permeated the air.

But this time, the sandbags along the front side of the property — covered in one long, extended piece of plastic — held strong, as did the retaining wall Scott had installed. There was no new flooding.

"Everything held pretty good," McCoy, Huntington Beach's fire chief, told reporters.

But he noted that the city was getting preliminary estimates that the tides could be even higher Thursday.

"We just don't want to let our guard down," he said.

Forecasters warn that more extreme coastal flooding is possible Thursday in Orange and San Diego counties. Major impacts could also be seen in L.A. and Ventura counties, the Central Coast and the San Francisco Bay Area, and moderate impacts are expected in L.A. County, Santa Barbara County and the Monterey Bay area.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .
authors: Rong-Gong Lin II, Fedor Zarkhin, Jenny Jarvie

articles.title: Has global jihadism failed, or is it simply changing shape?
articles.summary: Jihadist groups appear to be focusing on local issues rather than global terror. Does it signify a real change?
articles.body:
The group, which controls large parts of rural southern and central Somalia, has been keen to show off its so-called humanitarian work throughout 2026.

"May God reward them," said a local woman in one of al-Shabab's videos.

It's all part of an effort to win over local communities and present itself as more than just a jihadist group.

A quarter of a century after al-Qaeda's 9/11 attacks in the US, and 12 years after Islamic State group (IS) declared its so-called caliphate in Iraq and Syria, the jihadist movement looks very different.

Rather than focusing on attacking the West or fighting for a global Islamic state, some - especially those linked to al-Qaeda - are putting more effort into winning power closer to home. And they seem increasingly willing to make compromises along the way.

Because of this, a debate is growing within the movement. While hardliners reject compromise, pragmatists see working with local groups and former enemies as a way to gain power. But do the pragmatists represent a genuine change or simply a shift in tactics to achieve the same ultimate goals: establishing a state that applies their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law both at home and in its dealings with the outside world?

Neither al-Qaeda nor IS has achieved its ultimate dream: taking over one or more countries and ruling them according to their strict interpretation of Islam.

Both have suffered major defeats, lost leaders and faced years of international pressure. IS, which once controlled vast areas of Iraq and Syria, lost its last territorial stronghold in 2019. But jihadism hasn't gone away.

Africa is now the main battleground for jihadism, with al-Qaeda's powerful branches, JNIM in the Sahel (Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger) and al-Shabab in Somalia, fighting long-running insurgencies. IS, its bitter rival, has active branches in Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Sahel, Mozambique and Somalia.

One major source of inspiration, and envy, whether jihadists admit it or not, is Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa . The former IS and then al-Qaeda commander was once wanted by the US but rose to power in Syria in December 2024 and was welcomed by Western leaders.

Once known by his militant nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani, he led the jihadist group Nusra Front - initially linked to IS and then al-Qaeda - and later the group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS).

He gradually broke ties with both IS and al-Qaeda and distanced himself from their calls for global jihad.

Instead, he focused on Syria, building a local power base in the north-western Idlib province.

What surprised everyone was his growing willingness to work with non-Islamist groups and engage with foreign powers. As HTS advanced on Damascus, its leadership sought to reassure the international community, reaching out even to Russia, a key ally of then-president Bashar al-Assad, to allay fears of an Islamist takeover.

That pragmatism, combined with favourable geopolitical conditions - including a weaker Russia and Iran - helped him take power in Syria.

But the sight of him being welcomed by world leaders, including US President Donald Trump, was even more remarkable.

During Sharaa's visit to the White House in November 2025, Trump sprayed him with his own branded cologne, jokingly asked how many wives he had and praised him as a "very strong leader".

For some jihadists, Sharaa's success has been inspiring. Others, however, see his actions as a betrayal of everything they believe in.

IS has declared jihad against Syria's new Islamist government, branding Sharaa and his officials "apostates", and has carried out attacks against government forces on that basis. Other hardline clerics have taken a similar stance, but have stopped short of openly calling for jihad against Sharaa.

The divide between hardline jihadists and their more pragmatic counterparts has fuelled a bitter online debate since 2025, with rival voices trading accusations of betrayal and even publishing competing books to defend their positions.

For hardliners, going too far can mean abandoning their core beliefs. This might include holding back from imposing their strict version of Islamic law, accepting "man-made" laws or a constitution, taking part in elections, working with non-Islamist groups, or building ties with governments they consider "infidel".

Another source of inspiration for jihadists was the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan in 2021, as it showed that an Islamist movement could eventually take control of a country after years of fighting Western-backed forces. It engaged local groups, slowly secured power across the country, used international diplomacy, and bided its time before taking the capital, Kabul, in a lightning offensive.

Two groups are especially worth watching: al-Qaeda's branches in Mali and Somalia.

In late April, al-Qaeda's Sahel branch, known as JNIM, showed considerable pragmatism by joining forces with nationalist Tuareg separatists - whom it had occasionally fought - to launch a major offensive that threatened Mali's military rulers. It even went as far as to call the Tuaregs "brothers".

But it's not just JNIM's growing military strength that's attracting attention. It's also how the group is presenting itself.

Its propaganda once prominently featured al-Qaeda's leaders, slogans and calls for global jihad. Since late 2024, however, its videos have dropped the familiar al-Qaeda branding.

And instead of talking about global Muslim causes, JNIM has increasingly focused on local problems, portraying itself as a defender of ordinary people against corrupt and abusive rulers.

It has repeatedly accused Mali's military government and its Russian allies of killing civilians and making people's lives worse.

In April, it appealed to "all sincere patriots" to help build a "new Mali", promising security, justice and prosperity alongside Islamic law.

It has even suggested it could have "balanced relations" with Russia, despite the fact they're fighting Russian forces backing Mali's government. Its wording echoed that of HTS to Russia as it advanced on Damascus.

There are parallels with Sharaa's approach in Syria: build local alliances, reassure potential enemies and avoid giving outside powers a reason to intervene.

Africa security specialist Aman Bezreh sees similarities between the two groups, but says JNIM's shift may take time.

"JNIM has indeed shown signs of pragmatism similar to HTS", she says. "However, its rebranding has progressed more slowly because the group is simultaneously focused on expanding into new territories and recruiting from diverse pools."

The debate over which path to follow is also taking place within JNIM's leadership, according to Wassim Nasr, a France 24 journalist and jihadism expert.

He says one camp favours the Taliban's approach of taking power through force with minimal concessions. The other, which he says currently has the upper hand, favours an approach closer to that of Syria's HTS - making compromises and building wider alliances to gain power more quickly.

Nasr believes JNIM may borrow from both models, but that a break with al-Qaeda is inevitable as a result of its political evolution.

Like JNIM, al-Shabab in Somalia appears willing to make deals with former enemies.

According to Abdullahi Guji, BBC Monitoring's Somalia specialist, al-Shabab reached a truce in October with a powerful Somali tribe, the Ma'awisley, whose fighters had been at the forefront of the fight against the group.

The tribe has since withdrawn its fighters from the front line, dealing a serious blow to the government's campaign against jihadists, says Guji.

Guji believes the group may soon have a chance to test whether it can seize power and establish itself as an alternative government across wider parts of the country.

African Union forces are withdrawing from Somalia amid funding cuts and the approaching end of their mandate in December. Meanwhile, the Somali government is facing political crises and rebellions, creating vulnerabilities al-Shabab could exploit, he adds.

There's another reason some jihadists may see an opportunity to expand: they believe Western governments have bigger fish to fry.

With the war in Ukraine, US-Iran conflict in the Middle East and growing rivalries with China and Russia, fighting jihadists is no longer the priority it was after 9/11.

The US withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 and the Taliban's return to power, followed by Sharaa's rise in Syria, have reinforced that belief.

Colin Clarke, executive director of the Soufan Center, a non-profit research group that focuses on security, says some jihadist groups have learnt that avoiding confrontation with the US can help them escape Western military action and "live to fight another day".

That doesn't mean the West has stopped fighting terrorism. But if jihadists believe it is distracted or less willing to intervene, they may feel emboldened to pursue power.

Unlike its fiercely uncompromising rival IS, al-Qaeda has long shown some flexibility in pursuing its goals. But history offers a warning.

After the 2011 Arab uprisings, which largely sidelined al-Qaeda, affiliated jihadist groups in Yemen, Libya and Tunisia began using the name Ansar al-Sharia (Supporters of Sharia) to win local support without carrying the al-Qaeda brand.

In Mali in 2012, al-Qaeda leaders advised jihadists who had seized the north alongside Tuareg separatists not to rush into imposing strict Islamic rules. Instead, they urged them to work with local allies, avoid alienating communities and play down their al-Qaeda links.

The message wasn't to give up their ambitions. It was to show strategic patience until the time was right. That same thinking could be at work today.

Democrats have an identity crisis - it won't be an easy fix

Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin

Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them?

So are these groups really changing their ambitions, or just their tactics? Even those advocating compromise aren't necessarily abandoning their dream of establishing a state ruled by their strict interpretation of Islamic law.

Clarke wonders whether this more pragmatic approach could be a "Trojan horse strategy" – a way for jihadist groups to gain power without giving up their longer-term goals.

"The big question is whether being in power actually moderates these groups, or whether they're simply changing their tactics to survive and strengthen their position," he says.

IS remains firmly committed to its global ambitions and rejects compromise. Al-Qaeda's Yemen branch, AQAP, continues to call for attacks against the US and Israel, and urges "lone wolf" attacks against Western and Jewish targets.

And it's too early to say whether groups like JNIM and al-Shabab will follow the Taliban or Syrian examples, and whether they're willing to make compromises.

Some jihadist groups may become more focused on local politics as they face the challenges of governing. Others may simply be hiding their wider ambitions until they're strong enough to pursue them.

The global jihadist dream may have failed, but jihadism is far from finished.

articles.title: MIT historian investigates a Chinese tea label believed to be a Boston Tea Party relic for decades and traces it to a 19th-century American trading company
articles.summary: A Chinese tea chest label displayed for decades as a souvenir of the 1773 Boston Tea Party has been found to date from the 1860s or 1870s, following an
articles.body: A Chinese tea chest label displayed for decades as a souvenir of the 1773 Boston Tea Party has been found to date from the 1860s or 1870s, following an investigation by MIT historian Tristan G. Brown. The label, donated to Boston’s Old South Meeting House in 1987 by descendants of blacksmith Thomas Wells, was believed to have been recovered during the historic protest. However, Brown’s examination of its Chinese inscriptions, read in Cantonese rather than Mandarin, revealed the name of Smith, Archer & Co., an American trading firm operating in East Asia. His research traced the artefact to 19th-century tea commerce and uncovered how a family story became accepted as revolutionary history.How an MIT historian began investigating the mysterious Chinese tea labelAccording to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Brown began investigating the object after remembering it from a visit to the Old South Meeting House. The research project started in 2024, when the American Historical Review invited historians to examine 76 objects connected to 1776, the year the United States declared independence from Britain.Brown, a historian of China who does not usually work on American history, selected the Chinese label for further investigation. He initially had no reason to doubt the family’s account, particularly because objects directly connected to the Boston Tea Party are scarce. Participants in the protest had reasons to conceal their identities and avoid punishment by the British Crown.Cantonese translation cracks the mystery of a historic tea labelAccording to the study published in American Historical Review, titled ‘Tea Chest Label’, the breakthrough came through a closer examination of the Chinese characters printed on the label. Earlier researchers had approached the text through Mandarin, but Brown recognised that a sequence of characters was being used phonetically to represent a foreign company’s name.When read in Cantonese, the characters produced the words "Smith, Archer", identifying Smith, Archer & Co., a New York-based import-export firm with offices in East Asia during the 1860s and 1870s. The company acquired Chinese and Japanese teas for shipment to American markets.The label also mentioned Yuan Tianbo, a Cantonese merchant connected to the trading network. Brown traced the merchant to Yokohama, Japan, in the 1860s. These findings established that the document belonged to the commercial networks of 19th-century Pacific trade rather than the tea-trading system operating during the American colonial period.Family tea store offers clues to the origins of a historic Chinese labelAfter identifying Smith, Archer & Co., Brown investigated how the label might have entered the Wells family’s possession. His research led him to John Milton Wells, a relative who travelled from Michigan to the San Francisco Bay Area during the California Gold Rush, between 1848 and 1855.Although John Milton Wells did not find gold, he returned to Michigan and worked as a grocer. He also operated a business listed in commercial directories as the "California Tea Store". A surviving trade card associated with Wells advertised imported Asian teas. Brown examined it alongside family letters, census records and local business directories. Together, these documents indicated the label was likely acquired through the family's 19th-century tea business rather than recovered during the Boston Tea Party.Chinese tea label became mistaken for a Boston Tea Party relicBrown also investigated how the object became associated with the 1773 protest. He argued that its revolutionary connection probably developed later, during the centennial commemorations of the 1870s, when American families were emphasising their connections to the country's founding period.By the early 1900s, the story had appeared in a local newspaper, which reported that the label had been taken from a tea chest during the Boston Tea Party. Repeated accounts in family histories, newspapers, commemorative culture and eventually museum interpretation helped establish the claim as an apparently authoritative historical account.In his research, Brown explained that the label demonstrated how 19th-century global trade, Asian migration and family storytelling helped reshape American revolutionary memory by creating objects that appeared to authenticate that history.MIT historian publishes study uncovering the true origins of a Chinese tea labelBrown's findings were published in an article titled Tea Chest Label in the June 2026 issue of the American Historical Review. The paper, published online on July 3, reconstructs the document's origins and examines how it entered the Wells family's collection before eventually reaching a Boston museum.The investigation also highlights how digitised commercial directories, searchable newspaper archives and linguistic research can help historians revisit objects whose histories have long been accepted. Brown's attention to Cantonese rather than Mandarin proved central to identifying the company behind the label.Although the label was not produced during the Revolutionary era, Brown said it remained an important educational artefact documenting China's longstanding trade with the Americas and the ways Americans have looked to China when telling stories about their own past.He said: "History is never finished. Even objects that have sat in museums for decades can reveal entirely new stories when we ask new questions."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Nvidia's China link: How US firms with Chinese owners are accessing advanced AI chips
articles.summary: Nvidia is supplying some of its most advanced artificial intelligence chips to US-based companies with Chinese ownership, a CBS News investigation has
articles.body: Nvidia is supplying some of its most advanced artificial intelligence chips to US-based companies with Chinese ownership, a CBS News investigation has found. The findings raise fresh questions about whether American export restrictions are effectively keeping sensitive technology out of China’s hands.The investigation identified at least two California-based companies with Chinese ownership that have access to Nvidia’s high-end chips. One is a preferred partner of the chipmaker and is owned by a Chinese company whose chief executive graduated from a military-run university in China. Another changed its name after its Chinese parent company was placed on a US government blacklist, CBS News reported.Some of the US-based firms have subsequently leased or sold advanced chips to companies in Southeast Asia, according to corporate records examined by CBS News.The report, based on dozens of corporate filings, court records and an examination of Nvidia’s business relationships dating back to 2023, said complex ownership structures and multiple layers of transactions have made it difficult to establish where the chips ultimately end up.Chinese-owned firm among Nvidia’s preferred partnersOne company identified in the investigation is RiCloud AI, a data centre firm based in San Jose, California, which appears on Nvidia’s list of preferred US partners.The designation gives RiCloud priority access to high-end chips used to train and run advanced AI models, as well as Nvidia’s software and technical support.Nvidia’s public filings classify sales to RiCloud AI Inc as US sales. However, the company’s parent, Yuxing InfoTech Investment Holdings Ltd, is headquartered in Shenzhen, China, and listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange, CBS News reported.Yuxing’s chief executive and co-owner, Cong Yu, holds a degree in National Defence Mobilisation from the People’s Liberation Army Command College, a university run by the Chinese military. Yu also heads a related RiCloud company in California.Yuxing chairman Li Qiang previously led data centre firm Global Switch Holdings, which Australia’s Department of Defence dropped as a provider in June 2024 over national security concerns.The US government has not accused RiCloud or Yuxing of wrongdoing.RiCloud secured partner status with Nvidia in December 2025, about 10 weeks after it was incorporated, and later became a preferred cloud partner.CBS News also examined RiCloud’s customers and found what it described as unusual deals involving companies that were not traditionally associated with high-performance computing.In one transaction, RiCloud signed a $120 million agreement this year to lease 300 Nvidia B300 servers to Agencia Comercial Spirits, a Taiwanese company primarily known for importing whisky.California firm changed name after Chinese parent was blacklistedThe investigation also examined Aivres, a California-based company that Nvidia lists as an “elite” compute partner, its highest tier of business relationship.Aivres was previously known as Inspur, the same name as its Chinese parent company. In March 2023, Chinese firms belonging to the Inspur group were added to a US federal blacklist of companies considered a security risk.The California subsidiary subsequently changed its name to Aivres. The company itself is not on the blacklist and continues to maintain a close relationship with Nvidia, CBS News reported.A New York Times analysis of trade records, published two months ago, found that Aivres exported at least $5.6 billion worth of advanced technology to Southeast Asia between April 2024 and February 2026.About $3 billion of those exports involved computers containing Nvidia’s Blackwell chips, which are restricted from being exported to China, NYT reported.The servers were supplied to two companies in Malaysia — Megaspeed and Aolani.Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company where Alice Huang was a senior executive, was placed on a US government blacklist this week. The company is under investigation by the Justice Department over allegations that it circumvented export restrictions by obtaining chips for use in China. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing.Alice Huang has been described by US intelligence officials as a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, but the Justice Department has said it has not reached a conclusion. Beijing has denied that she is a spy.Nvidia’s sales figures under scrutinyThe investigation also raised questions about Nvidia’s reporting of sales by region.The company previously disclosed sales according to the billing location of its customers. Those figures showed that in 2024, nearly half of its chip sales were billed to the US, 18% to Singapore and 13% to China.In November last year, Nvidia changed its reporting method to reflect customers’ headquarters rather than billing locations. The change revealed that an additional $7.9 billion in 2024 sales had been billed to companies headquartered in China, CBS News reported.In 2025, US-headquartered customers accounted for 69% of Nvidia’s sales, while China accounted for 9%.Nvidia’s filings state that “the end customer and shipping location may be different from our customers’ headquarters location”.CBS News said its findings suggested the change in reporting could make the actual destinations of Nvidia’s chips harder to determine.You use AI every day. The Public Prosecutor's office said DNA tests were being conducted to identify those killed.Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the injured had been taken to nearby hospitals and that he would visit the accident site. articles.title: ‘Irreversible reality’: Kim lays out North Korea's nuclear expansion plans after ignoring Trump's offer to meet
articles.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has called for expanding the country's nuclear weapons programme after inspecting two nuclear materials production
articles.body: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has called for expanding the country's nuclear weapons programme after inspecting two nuclear materials production facilities, reaffirming Pyongyang's determination to strengthen its atomic arsenal despite US President Donald Trump's latest offer to resume diplomatic engagement.Kim's visit to the facilities, one newly inaugurated and the other undergoing expansion, came after Trump expressed interest in meeting the North Korean leader during his recent Asia visit. However, Pyongyang did not publicly respond to the US president's overture, and no meeting took place.North Korea's state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) reported on Thursday that Kim inspected the facilities on Wednesday, accompanied by senior military officials. Photographs released by the agency showed Kim walking through halls containing rows of equipment believed to be centrifuges used for uranium enrichment. Other images appeared to show displays of nuclear warheads, although some photographs were blurred.KCNA also said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as part of the inspection.Kim said the visit was aimed at strengthening the country's defence capabilities in response to what he described as “variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment”.He accused the United States of encouraging its regional allies to acquire nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them.“The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality,” Kim said, according to KCNA.Kim also called for further development of North Korea's low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons, arguing that deploying such weapons across multiple domains for different military missions was essential given the country's security situation.He referred to South Korea as the “inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state”, underscoring Pyongyang's continued focus on its southern neighbour as a primary security threat.Kim seeks to strengthen nuclear capabilitiesKim's latest remarks reinforce his position that North Korea will not abandon its nuclear weapons programme, which has become central to the country's military strategy and political leadership.In recent years, he has accelerated the expansion of the programme following the collapse of high-level negotiations with Trump in 2019. The two leaders had held multiple rounds of diplomatic engagement during Trump's first presidential term, but their efforts failed to produce an agreement on denuclearisation and sanctions relief.North Korea has disclosed uranium enrichment facilities on only a few occasions. The country first revealed a facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010.Pyongyang has not disclosed the locations of the two facilities inspected by Kim this week. In June, when North Korea released images of parts of a uranium enrichment facility during another visit by Kim, outside experts assessed that it was likely an additional enrichment site that the country was suspected of developing at Yongbyon.Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director General Rafael Grossi said North Korea had been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon, describing the development as “a cause for serious concern.”Nuclear weapons can be produced using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium. North Korea has facilities to produce both materials at Yongbyon.Last year, South Korea's Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.Trump says meeting with Kim could happen laterTrump reiterated his willingness to resume diplomatic engagement with Kim during his visit to China last week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. However, the proposed meeting did not materialise, with North Korea making no public response to his offer.In an interview with the New York Post this week, Trump dismissed suggestions that Kim had ignored his outreach.“No, he didn’t ignore it. You know, we had many leaders there … There’ll be a time when we meet … It was just not really the right time. It was a very busy two-day period.”Trump also said he could revive diplomatic engagement with Kim at any time by restarting the exchange of letters that the two leaders maintained during his first term. However, he acknowledged that they had not corresponded “recently.”Kim has previously indicated that he could consider returning to negotiations if Washington abandons what Pyongyang describes as its “hostile policy” towards North Korea and recognises the country's status as a nuclear state.Experts believe Kim is seeking international recognition of North Korea as a nuclear-armed state, which could strengthen his position in negotiations and allow him to push for the lifting of international sanctions.North Korea strengthens ties with Russia, ChinaAlongside expanding its nuclear programme, Kim has increasingly shifted North Korea's foreign policy towards strengthening ties with its Cold War-era allies, Russia and China.The diplomatic shift followed the breakdown of negotiations with Washington in 2019 and has helped Pyongyang strengthen its regional position while pursuing its ambition of establishing North Korea as a permanent nuclear power.Kim's latest inspection and call for further nuclear weapons development indicate that Pyongyang remains committed to expanding its arsenal, even as Trump continues to express interest in restarting direct diplomacy.You use AI every day. articles.title: Netanyahu's corruption trial at a turning point? Israeli judges question key charges against PM
articles.summary: Israeli judges on Wednesday urged prosecutors to reconsider three corruption cases against prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
articles.body: Israeli judges on Wednesday urged prosecutors to reconsider three corruption cases against prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The judge stated that the chances of convicting him in one bribery case were low and questioned whether an offence had been committed in another, in a major setback for the long-running prosecution.The judges at the Jerusalem District Court summoned Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, who has the authority to decide whether the cases should proceed, and asked her to consider dropping one of the charges and reassessing the others.The panel said there was little likelihood of a conviction in Case 4,000, which alleges that Netanyahu granted regulatory favours to a telecommunications mogul in exchange for favourable coverage on a news website. The judges also expressed serious doubts over whether the alleged conduct in Case 2,000, involving a proposed deal with a newspaper publisher, amounted to a criminal offence.They left open the possibility of a conviction in Case 1,000, in which Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust for accepting gifts from wealthy businessmen in return for helping them with their interests.Baharav-Miara told the court that she and her team would consider the judges’ recommendations and remain open to all options based on the evidence, according to a transcript provided by a Justice Ministry spokeswoman to New York Times.The judges stressed that their remarks reflected their assessment of the evidence at this stage and did not amount to a verdict.Netanyahu, who has denied all wrongdoing and described the prosecution as a political witch hunt, said the trial had collapsed and called for it to end immediately.“Today, the trial has fallen,” he said in a televised statement, describing the judges’ comments as “a ray of truth and justice”.The prime minister said it had taken 10 years for the truth to emerge, referring to the investigations into his conduct that began about a decade ago. He also spoke of the “terrible suffering” endured by him and his family.Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate but interlocking cases. Prosecutors allege that he granted government and regulatory benefits to business figures in exchange for gifts and favourable media coverage for him and his family.Three cases at the centre of trialIn Case 4,000, Netanyahu is accused of helping the controlling shareholder of Israel’s largest telecommunications company, Bezeq, in return for positive coverage on the news website Walla, which the businessman owned. The judges said the chances of conviction in the bribery case were low enough to warrant reconsideration.Case 2,000 concerns an alleged backroom arrangement between Netanyahu and the owner of a popular daily newspaper. The proposed deal, which never came to fruition, would have involved favourable coverage of Netanyahu in exchange for measures against a rival publication. The judges said they had serious doubts that the evidence established a criminal offence.Case 1,000 involves allegations that Netanyahu accepted nearly $300,000 in gifts, including cigars and champagne, from Hollywood producer Arnon Milchan and Australian billionaire James Packer between 2007 and 2016.Prosecutors allege that Netanyahu sought to help Milchan extend a tax exemption and used his influence to assist him in renewing his US visa. The attorney general said the options in this case were either a verdict or a plea deal.Netanyahu completed his testimony in June, prompting the judges to take stock of the proceedings, which have been delayed over the years, including by the war in Gaza.Political future in the balanceThe development comes at a crucial moment for Netanyahu, whose political future has been thrown into uncertainty after last month’s election failed to produce a clear parliamentary majority.His rival, former military chief and centrist Gadi Eisenkot, has been given the first opportunity by Israel’s president to form a new government. Netanyahu and his allies won more seats than Eisenkot’s bloc but fell short of securing an outright majority.Netanyahu’s indictment and trial have contributed to years of political instability in Israel, with several mainstream parties refusing to join coalitions led by him, arguing that he is unfit to govern while facing criminal charges.The judges’ intervention could now give Netanyahu a significant political boost, though the cases remain before the court and no final decision has been made on whether they will be dropped or proceed to judgment.You use AI every day. articles.title: Black nurses left their homes and families to help a Vermont nursing home during the pandemic; four years after a federal lawsuit was filed over alleged racial harassment, Elderwood agrees to a $450,000 settlement
articles.summary: They travelled away from their homes and families during a global health emergency to help care for vulnerable residents, but some Black nurses and
articles.body: They travelled away from their homes and families during a global health emergency to help care for vulnerable residents, but some Black nurses and nursing assistants allegedly faced racial slurs, threats and physical attacks at the facility where they worked. Four years after a federal discrimination lawsuit was filed over the alleged treatment, a Vermont nursing home operator has agreed to pay $450,000 to settle the case and introduce measures to prevent further harassment.According to the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), which announced the settlement on November 24, 2026, 98 Starr Farm Road Operating Co., doing business as Elderwood at Burlington, and Elderwood Administrative Services LLC agreed to the financial settlement and additional workplace protections. The agreement resolves a federal lawsuit alleging that the companies failed to respond adequately to repeated racial harassment of Black employees by nursing-home residents.Black nurses faced racial harassment while working during the pandemicThe allegations concern employees at Elderwood at Burlington, a skilled nursing facility in Burlington, Vermont. According to the EEOC, the harassment began in 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, when the facility was dealing with staffing shortages. Most of the affected Black employees were travelling nurses who had left their homes and families to help the nursing home maintain its services during a difficult period. Instead of finding a supportive working environment, they allegedly encountered repeated racial abuse from some of the residents.The EEOC's lawsuit described incidents involving racial slurs, threats and physical attacks. One resident allegedly repeatedly told Black employees to return to Africa, followed them around the facility while directing racial abuse at them and physically assaulted several workers. Other incidents involved residents making threats of violence and expressing preferences against receiving care from Black employees.The agency alleged that nursing-home managers and supervisors knew about the incidents, either because they witnessed the behaviour or because employees reported it to them. However, the company allegedly failed to take sufficiently prompt and effective action to stop the harassment.How the federal discrimination lawsuit beganThe EEOC filed its lawsuit on September 6, 2022, in the US District Court for the District of Vermont. The case, EEOC v. 98 Starr Farm Road Operating Co., LLC, also named Elderwood Administrative Services LLC as a defendant. The agency argued that the alleged conduct created a racially hostile work environment in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The federal law prohibits employment discrimination based on race and requires employers to take appropriate action when they become aware of workplace harassment.An important issue in the case was that the alleged harassment came from nursing-home residents rather than supervisors or fellow employees. The EEOC maintained that employers still have responsibilities to protect workers from racial harassment by people they encounter while performing their jobs, including patients and residents.The defendants sought summary judgment, asking the court to resolve the case in their favour without a trial. However, on March 26, 2026, the federal district court denied that request. The court concluded that a reasonable jury could find that the workplace had been affected by severe or pervasive racial discrimination and that the defendants had failed to take sufficiently effective corrective action. This allowed the EEOC's hostile-work-environment claim to proceed towards trial.What the $450,000 settlement requiresThe settlement was reached before trial and is governed by a two-and-a-half-year consent decree. Under the agreement, the defendants will pay a total of $450,000 in monetary relief to the affected employees. The defendants denied the allegations and made no admission of liability under the consent decree. The financial payment is accompanied by several requirements aimed at preventing similar incidents. Elderwood must revise and distribute its anti-discrimination policy, establishing procedures for reporting, investigating and responding to racial harassment by residents and other people who are not employees.The company must also provide annual interactive anti-discrimination training to employees at the Burlington facility and its corporate office. Managers and supervisors will receive additional training on their responsibilities. Another significant requirement is a resident code of conduct that prohibits discrimination and harassment against employees. It will make clear that the facility will not accommodate requests to assign or exclude caregivers based on their race.The agreement also requires an independent hotline for discrimination complaints, notices to employees, an annual message from the Elderwood administrator reaffirming the company's commitment to a harassment-free workplace and periodic compliance reports. The EEOC will monitor the defendants' compliance throughout the decree's term.EEOC officials said the settlement reinforces the responsibility of healthcare and long-term care employers to respond to racial harassment, regardless of whether the alleged perpetrators are employees, patients or residents. The agreement brings the four-year federal lawsuit to a resolution without a trial verdict on the discrimination allegations, while requiring Elderwood to compensate the affected workers and strengthen its policies for protecting employees.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2015, MP man buys TV for Rs 31,500 with 3-year warranty, alleges it stopped displaying pictures in 2018; claims company ignored toll-free complaint, state consumer commission rejects appeal over lack of proof
